prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Vortices are pervasive in nature, representing the breakdown of laminar fluid flow and hence playing a key role in turbulence. The fluid rotation associated with a vortex can be parameterized by the circulation $\Gamma=\oint {\rm d}{\bf r}\cdot{\bf v}({\bf r})$ about the vortex, where ${\bf v}({\bf r})$ is the fluid velocity field. While classical vortices can take any value of circulation, superfluids are irrotational, and any rotation or angular momentum is constrained to occur through vortices with quantized circulation. Quantized vortices also play a key role in the dissipation of transport in superfluids. In BECs quantized vortices have been observed in several forms, including single vortices, vortex lattices, and vortex pairs and rings. The recent observation of quantized vortices in a fermionic gas was taken as a clear signature of the underlying condensation and superfluidity of fermion pairs. In addition to BECs, quantized vortices also occur in superfluid Helium, nonlinear optics, and type-II superconductors.

Vortices occur widely throughout nature and arise when smooth, laminar fluid motion breaks down, making them central to turbulent behavior. The rotational motion of fluid around a vortex is characterized by the circulation
\[
\Gamma=\oint {\rm d}{\bf r}\cdot{\bf v}({\bf r}),
\]
where \({\bf v}({\bf r})\) denotes the fluid’s velocity field and the integral is evaluated along a closed path surrounding the vortex. In ordinary fluids, circulation may assume any value. Superfluids, however, are irrotational, so their rotation and angular momentum can exist only through vortices whose circulation is quantized. These quantized vortices are also important mechanisms for transport dissipation in superfluids.

In Bose–Einstein condensates (BECs), experiments have detected quantized vortices as isolated vortices, vortex lattices, paired vortices, and vortex rings. Their recent observation in a fermionic gas was regarded as strong evidence for both condensation and superfluidity of paired fermions. Quantized vortices are not limited to BECs; they are also found in superfluid helium, nonlinear optical systems, and type-II superconductors.

Vortices are a hallmark of the breakdown of smooth, laminar fluid flow and play a central role in the onset and dynamics of turbulence. They consist of regions in which the fluid circulates around a core. The strength of this rotational motion is characterized by the circulation,

\[
\Gamma=\oint_C \mathbf{v}\cdot d\mathbf{l},
\]

where \(\mathbf{v}\) is the fluid velocity and the integral is taken around a closed contour \(C\) enclosing the vortex.

In classical fluids, circulation can vary continuously. By contrast, an irrotational superfluid can sustain vortices only with quantized circulation. Because the superfluid velocity is related to the phase of a macroscopic quantum wavefunction, the requirement that this wavefunction remain single-valued restricts the circulation to integer multiples of a fundamental quantum:

\[
\Gamma=n\frac{h}{m},
\]

where \(n\) is an integer and \(m\) is the mass of the condensed particle—or the mass of a pair in a paired fermionic superfluid. Although the flow is irrotational away from the vortex core, the phase winds by \(2\pi n\) around the core, where the superfluid density is strongly suppressed.

Quantized vortices strongly influence the transport properties of quantum fluids. Their motion, creation, and interaction with excitations can produce dissipation even though the underlying fluid is superfluid. In Bose–Einstein condensates, they have been observed in many configurations, including isolated vortices, ordered vortex lattices, vortex–antivortex pairs, and three-dimensional vortex rings.

The phenomenon is not limited to bosonic condensates. Quantized vortices also occur in ultracold fermionic gases, superfluid helium, nonlinear optical systems, and type-II superconductors, where magnetic flux penetrates the material through quantized vortex lines. In fermionic gases in particular, the observation of quantized vortices provides compelling evidence for pair condensation and superfluidity, since the vortices reflect the existence of a coherent macroscopic phase associated with paired fermions.

Vortices are a hallmark of the transition from smooth, laminar motion to more complex fluid behavior. In a classical fluid, a vortex is a region in which the flow circulates around a central core. Its strength is measured by the circulation,
\[
\Gamma=\oint_{\mathcal C}\mathbf{v}\cdot d\mathbf{l},
\]
where \(\mathbf{v}\) is the fluid velocity and the integral is taken around a closed contour \(\mathcal C\). Classical circulation can generally vary continuously, allowing vortices to possess a broad range of strengths and structures.

The situation is fundamentally different in a superfluid. Away from vortex cores, the superfluid velocity is determined by the phase \(\phi\) of a macroscopic complex order parameter and is therefore irrotational. Because this phase must return to the same value, up to an integer multiple of \(2\pi\), after a closed path around a vortex, the circulation is restricted to discrete values:
\[
\Gamma=n\frac{h}{m},
\]
where \(n\) is an integer, \(h\) is Planck’s constant, and \(m\) is the relevant particle or pair mass. At the vortex core, the density or order-parameter amplitude is suppressed, allowing the phase to become undefined and the circulation to remain nonzero despite the irrotational flow elsewhere.

Quantized vortices arise in many systems described by a coherent macroscopic wave function. They have been observed in atomic Bose–Einstein condensates, paired fermionic gases, and superfluid helium. Closely related phase singularities occur in nonlinear optical fields, while type-II superconductors support vortices that carry quantized magnetic flux. In rotating superfluids, large numbers of vortices commonly form ordered lattices whose average motion approximates rigid-body rotation.

These vortices provide the primary means by which superfluids carry angular momentum. Their nucleation, motion, interaction, reconnection, and decay also play central roles in dissipation, turbulence, and the loss of persistent flow. Because quantized circulation follows directly from a single-valued macroscopic phase, observing quantized vortices offers compelling evidence for condensation, phase coherence, and superfluid or superconducting behavior.

## Vortices and Gamma

Vortices are rotating structures found throughout nature, from spiraling water and atmospheric storms to plasma flows and distant galaxies. At the center of vortex dynamics is **gamma**, commonly written as **Γ**, which represents circulation—the total rotational motion of a fluid around a closed path.

The value of Γ helps describe a vortex’s strength. A larger gamma indicates stronger circulation and usually higher flow velocities around the vortex core. In an ideal fluid, circulation can remain constant as the vortex moves or changes shape, an idea expressed by Kelvin’s circulation theorem.

Understanding vortices and gamma is essential in aerodynamics, meteorology, oceanography, and physics. Together, they reveal how rotational motion forms, evolves, and transports energy through complex systems.

In Bose–Einstein condensates, the circulation quantum is typically \(h/m\), where \(m\) is the boson mass; in fermionic superfluids, where pairing produces composite bosons, it is \(h/(2m)\). Quantized vortices therefore provide a direct signature of superfluidity in both ultracold Bose and Fermi gases.

counterfactuals.prompt: What are quantized vortices, how is circulation defined mathematically, and why are vortices considered evidence of superfluidity?
counterfactuals.output:
**Quantized vortices** are topological defects in a superfluid’s macroscopic quantum wavefunction. Writing the order parameter as

\[
\Psi(\mathbf r)=\sqrt{n_s(\mathbf r)}\,e^{i\theta(\mathbf r)},
\]

the superfluid velocity is related to its phase by

\[
\mathbf v_s=\frac{\hbar}{m}\nabla\theta,
\]

where \(m\) is the mass of the condensed particle—or the pair mass in a paired superfluid.

### Circulation

The circulation around a closed contour \(C\) is

\[
\Gamma=\oint_C \mathbf v_s\cdot d\boldsymbol{\ell}.
\]

Because the wavefunction must be single-valued, its phase change around the loop must be an integer multiple of \(2\pi\):

\[
\oint_C \nabla\theta\cdot d\boldsymbol{\ell}=2\pi n,
\qquad n\in\mathbb Z.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\boxed{\Gamma=n\frac{h}{m}}.
\]

For paired fermions, such as superfluid helium-3 or superconducting electron pairs, \(m\) is the pair mass, so the circulation quantum is \(h/(2m_{\rm constituent})\).

At the vortex core, the density falls toward zero, allowing the phase to be undefined. Outside the core, the flow is locally irrotational,

\[
\nabla\times\mathbf v_s=0,
\]

yet a loop enclosing the core has nonzero quantized circulation.

### Why this indicates superfluidity

Ordinary fluids can also contain vortices, but their circulation is generally continuous rather than restricted to discrete values. Quantized vortices indicate:

- a coherent macroscopic quantum phase;
- single-valuedness of the superfluid order parameter;
- persistent, topologically protected circulation;
- the characteristic response of a rotating superfluid, which forms a vortex array rather than rotating as an ordinary rigid body.

Thus, observing **discrete circulation quanta**, vortex lattices, or related effects is strong evidence for superfluidity, although the mere presence of nonquantized vortical flow would not be sufficient.

counterfactuals.prompt: Provide a textbook-style overview of classical versus quantum vortices, including their role in turbulence, transport dissipation, and experimental observations in BECs.
counterfactuals.output:
# Classical and Quantum Vortices

A **vortex** is a region of rotational fluid motion characterized by circulating flow around a core. Vortices occur in ordinary viscous fluids, plasmas, superfluids, superconductors, and atomic Bose–Einstein condensates (BECs). Classical and quantum vortices share broad dynamical features—circulation, interactions, reconnections, and turbulence—but differ fundamentally in their microscopic structure and allowed circulation.

## 1. Classical vortices

For a classical fluid with velocity field \(\mathbf v(\mathbf r,t)\), the local rotational motion is described by the **vorticity**

\[
\boldsymbol{\omega}=\nabla\times \mathbf v.
\]

A vortex is a region where \(\boldsymbol{\omega}\neq 0\). The circulation around a closed contour \(C\) is

\[
\Gamma=\oint_C \mathbf v\cdot d\mathbf l
      =\int_S \boldsymbol{\omega}\cdot d\mathbf S,
\]

where the second equality follows from Stokes’s theorem.

### 1.1 Continuous circulation and core structure

In a classical fluid, circulation is generally a continuous quantity: it can take arbitrary values determined by the initial and boundary conditions. Vorticity may also be distributed smoothly over a finite region rather than concentrated on a single line.

An idealized straight vortex with circulation \(\Gamma\) has azimuthal velocity

\[
v_\theta(r)=\frac{\Gamma}{2\pi r}
\]

outside its core. Real fluids regularize the apparent divergence at \(r=0\) through a finite vortex core, within which the velocity and vorticity remain finite.

### 1.2 Vortex dynamics

In an inviscid, barotropic fluid, Kelvin’s circulation theorem states that circulation around a material contour is conserved. In viscous fluids, however, vorticity diffuses according to terms proportional to the kinematic viscosity \(\nu\).

Three-dimensional classical vortices can undergo:

- **advection** by the background flow,
- **stretching and tilting**,
- **interaction and reconnection**,
- **viscous diffusion and decay**.

Vortex stretching is especially important in three-dimensional classical turbulence. Stretching a vortex tube reduces its cross-sectional area and increases its vorticity, helping transfer kinetic energy toward smaller scales.

---

## 2. Quantum vortices

Quantum vortices occur in systems described by a macroscopic complex order parameter,

\[
\Psi(\mathbf r,t)=\sqrt{n(\mathbf r,t)}\,e^{i\phi(\mathbf r,t)},
\]

where \(n\) is the particle density and \(\phi\) is the condensate phase. For particles of mass \(m\), the superfluid velocity is

\[
\mathbf v_s=\frac{\hbar}{m}\nabla\phi.
\]

Because the phase must return to itself modulo \(2\pi\) after going around a closed loop,

\[
\oint \nabla\phi\cdot d\mathbf l=2\pi q,
\]

where \(q\) is an integer. Therefore,

\[
\Gamma=\oint \mathbf v_s\cdot d\mathbf l
      =q\frac{h}{m}
      =q\kappa,
\]

with

\[
\kappa=\frac{h}{m}
\]

the quantum of circulation.

Thus, unlike classical circulation, superfluid circulation is **quantized**.

### 2.1 Phase singularity and vortex core

Away from vortex cores,

\[
\nabla\times \mathbf v_s=0,
\]

so superfluid flow is locally irrotational. Nevertheless, a contour enclosing a vortex can have nonzero circulation because the phase is singular along the vortex core.

The condensate density must fall to zero at the core so that the order parameter remains well defined. The characteristic core radius in a weakly interacting BEC is of order the **healing length**

\[
\xi=\frac{\hbar}{\sqrt{2mgn}},
\]

where \(g\) is the interaction coefficient and \(n\) is the bulk density.

Outside the core, a singly quantized vortex has approximately

\[
v_\theta(r)=\frac{\hbar}{mr}
           =\frac{\kappa}{2\pi r}.
\]

Singly quantized vortices, \(q=\pm1\), are normally energetically favored. A multiply quantized vortex often splits into several singly quantized vortices unless it is stabilized by geometry or external pinning.

### 2.2 Dimensionality

In three dimensions, quantum vortices form lines or closed loops. In two-dimensional or highly oblate systems, they behave approximately as point-like topological defects. Their sign is set by the direction of phase winding.

Quantum vortex lines can:

- move under the local superfluid flow,
- interact through their velocity fields,
- reconnect when they approach,
- support helical **Kelvin waves**,
- form polarized bundles or disordered tangles.

---

## 3. Main differences

| Property | Classical vortex | Quantum vortex |
|---|---|---|
| Circulation | Continuous | Quantized: \(\Gamma=q h/m\) |
| Vorticity | Usually distributed over a finite region | Concentrated at singular vortex lines or cores |
| Core scale | Set by viscosity, forcing, and flow history | Set mainly by healing or coherence length |
| Velocity field | Determined by vorticity distribution | Fixed circulation for each winding number |
| Dissipation | Directly affected by viscosity | Superfluid component is inviscid, but vortices can dissipate through other channels |
| Vortex stretching | Central in 3D turbulence | Line length can grow, but circulation per vortex remains fixed |
| Topology | Not generally protected | Protected by phase winding unless the vortex exits, annihilates, or undergoes reconnection |

The distinction is not absolute at large scales. A collection of many aligned quantum vortices can mimic a continuous classical vorticity field when coarse-grained over distances much larger than the intervortex spacing.

---

# 4. Vortices and turbulence

## 4.1 Classical turbulence

Classical turbulence is characterized by irregular motion over a broad range of length and time scales. In three-dimensional turbulence, energy is commonly injected at a large scale \(L\), transferred through an inertial range, and dissipated at small scales by viscosity.

Kolmogorov’s theory predicts the energy spectrum

\[
E(k)\sim C\varepsilon^{2/3}k^{-5/3},
\]

where \(k\) is the wavenumber and \(\varepsilon\) is the energy-transfer rate per unit mass.

Vortices are central to this process. Stretching and folding produce thinner, more intense vortex structures, while reconnections and viscous effects generate fine scales. At sufficiently small scales, viscosity converts kinetic energy into heat.

In two dimensions, vortex dynamics differ because ordinary vortex stretching is absent. Energy may undergo an **inverse cascade** toward larger scales, while enstrophy is transferred toward smaller scales. Long-lived coherent vortices are consequently common in two-dimensional turbulence.

## 4.2 Quantum turbulence

**Quantum turbulence** is a turbulent state containing many interacting quantized vortices. In three dimensions it often appears as a tangled network of vortex lines; in two dimensions it may consist of a disordered gas of vortices and antivortices.

Two broad regimes are often distinguished:

1. **Quasiclassical turbulence**  
   Vortices become partially polarized into bundles, and the large-scale flow resembles classical turbulence. A \(k^{-5/3}\)-like energy spectrum can appear on scales larger than the mean intervortex spacing.

2. **Ultraquantum or Vinen turbulence**  
   The vortex tangle is less organized and lacks strong large-scale flow. The dynamics are dominated more directly by individual lines, loops, and reconnections.

At scales below the intervortex spacing, classical continuous-vorticity descriptions fail. Energy can instead be transferred through:

- vortex reconnections,
- Kelvin-wave excitations along vortex lines,
- fragmentation into smaller vortex loops,
- emission of density waves or phonons.

A proposed low-temperature route to dissipation is a **Kelvin-wave cascade**, in which increasingly short-wavelength distortions form on vortex lines until their energy can be radiated as phonons.

In two-dimensional quantum fluids, vortex–antivortex interactions are particularly important. Opposite-sign vortices can form dipoles and annihilate, while like-sign vortices may cluster. Under suitable conditions, clustering can produce large-scale circulation analogous to the inverse energy cascade of classical two-dimensional turbulence.

---

# 5. Transport and dissipation

## 5.1 Classical fluids

Momentum transport in a Newtonian fluid is governed by viscosity. The Navier–Stokes equation contains the dissipative term

\[
\nu\nabla^2\mathbf v.
\]

The kinetic-energy dissipation rate per unit mass is related to velocity gradients and is often written schematically as

\[
\varepsilon \sim \nu \langle |\nabla \mathbf v|^2\rangle.
\]

Vortices enhance dissipation by generating strong velocity gradients and by carrying energy to scales where viscosity becomes effective. They also strongly influence:

- drag on objects,
- mixing of heat and particles,
- wake formation,
- momentum transport,
- boundary-layer separation.

## 5.2 Superfluids and BECs

An ideal zero-temperature superfluid has no conventional shear viscosity. This does not mean that all flows are nondissipative. A flow can lose energy through the creation and motion of excitations, especially after exceeding a critical velocity.

Important dissipation mechanisms include:

- nucleation and shedding of quantized vortices,
- vortex reconnections,
- sound or phonon emission,
- Kelvin-wave radiation,
- vortex–antivortex annihilation,
- scattering from thermal excitations,
- loss of vortices at system boundaries.

At finite temperature, a superfluid is often described using superfluid and normal components. Interaction between vortex lines and the normal component produces **mutual friction**. This damps vortex motion and transfers momentum and energy between the two components.

In dilute atomic BECs, finite-temperature damping can be modeled approximately by dissipative extensions of the Gross–Pitaevskii equation or by kinetic theories coupling the condensate to a thermal cloud. The observed decay of vortex number or turbulence therefore depends on temperature, trap geometry, dimensionality, and atom loss.

### 5.3 Critical velocity

According to the Landau criterion, excitations become energetically possible when the flow velocity exceeds

\[
v_c=\min_p\frac{\epsilon(p)}{p}.
\]

In real trapped systems, vortex nucleation often occurs below the ideal Landau value because boundaries, obstacles, density inhomogeneity, and surface modes lower the practical critical velocity. Vortex shedding behind an obstacle provides an important mechanism for drag in an otherwise superfluid system.

---

# 6. Experimental observations in atomic BECs

Atomic BECs provide unusually direct access to quantum vortices because the order parameter, interactions, geometry, and external forcing can be controlled.

## 6.1 Creation of vortices

Vortices have been generated by several methods:

- rotating an anisotropic trapping potential,
- stirring with a focused laser beam,
- moving a repulsive obstacle through the condensate,
- phase imprinting,
- merging condensates with different phases,
- rapidly quenching through the condensation transition,
- transferring orbital angular momentum with light.

When a condensate is rotated above a threshold frequency, many vortices enter and arrange into a triangular **Abrikosov lattice**. Although originally associated with type-II superconductors, the same lattice geometry follows from the repulsive effective interaction between like-signed vortices in a rotating superfluid.

The coarse-grained vortex density obeys the Feynman relation

\[
n_v \kappa \simeq 2\Omega,
\]

or

\[
n_v\simeq \frac{2\Omega}{\kappa},
\]

where \(\Omega\) is the angular rotation frequency. Thus a dense vortex lattice reproduces rigid-body rotation on average, even though the microscopic superfluid flow remains irrotational away from each core.

## 6.2 Detection and imaging

A vortex core is typically comparable to the healing length and may be difficult to resolve in situ. Common detection methods include:

- **time-of-flight expansion**, which enlarges the core before absorption imaging;
- **in situ phase-contrast or high-resolution imaging**;
- **interferometry**, which reveals phase winding through fork-like fringe dislocations;
- **tomographic imaging**, used to reconstruct three-dimensional vortex lines;
- repeated, minimally destructive imaging to track vortex trajectories.

A density depletion alone is not always sufficient to establish a vortex because sound pulses or other excitations can also create density minima. Evidence of phase circulation or dynamical behavior strengthens the identification.

## 6.3 Observed vortex phenomena

BEC experiments have demonstrated:

- isolated singly and multiply quantized vortices,
- splitting of unstable multiply quantized vortices,
- vortex dipoles and vortex–antivortex annihilation,
- precession of off-center vortices,
- regular vortex lattices,
- disordered vortex configurations and vortex tangles,
- vortex shedding behind moving obstacles,
- reconnections of vortex lines,
- Kelvin-wave-like excitations,
- decay of vortex number at finite temperature,
- clustering and signatures of two-dimensional turbulent cascades.

In highly oblate BECs, experiments probe two-dimensional vortex physics, including the Berezinskii–Kosterlitz–Thouless mechanism. In this picture, low-temperature vortices and antivortices are predominantly bound in pairs, while thermal unbinding of pairs destroys quasi-long-range phase coherence.

## 6.4 Turbulence experiments

Quantum turbulence in BECs can be produced by oscillatory stirring, trap deformation, rapid rotation changes, quenches, or collisions between condensates. Experimental signatures include:

- irregular vortex distributions,
- broad momentum distributions,
- enhanced density fluctuations,
- power-law energy or occupation spectra,
- changing vortex-number statistics,
- anisotropic or self-similar expansion,
- the growth and decay of coherence lengths.

Interpretation requires care because atomic gases are finite, trapped, and often inhomogeneous. Their accessible range of length scales may be too narrow for an unambiguous inertial-range power law. Consequently, vortex imaging, correlation functions, energy decomposition, and dynamical scaling are usually considered together.

---

# 7. Unifying perspective

Classical and quantum vortices represent two realizations of rotational fluid dynamics. In classical fluids, vorticity is a continuous field and viscosity ultimately dissipates turbulent energy. In quantum fluids, vorticity is carried by discrete topological defects with fixed circulation. Despite this microscopic difference, sufficiently dense or organized collections of quantum vortices can reproduce classical behavior at large scales.

The most important crossover is set by the mean intervortex spacing:

- **Above that scale**, coarse-grained quantum turbulence may show classical flow structures and Kolmogorov-like cascades.
- **Below that scale**, individual vortex cores, reconnections, Kelvin waves, and phonon emission dominate.

BECs are especially valuable because they permit controlled preparation and direct imaging of these processes. They therefore serve both as quantum many-body systems and as laboratory models for broad questions about turbulence, topological defects, transport, and dissipation.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the significance of quantized vortices in quantum fluids and mention examples of systems in which they occur, such as superfluid helium, nonlinear optics, and type-II superconductors.
counterfactuals.output:
Quantized vortices are topological defects in quantum fluids where the phase of a macroscopic wavefunction winds by an integer multiple of \(2\pi\) around a vortex core. This produces discrete circulation,

\[
\oint \mathbf{v}\cdot d\mathbf{l}=n\frac{h}{m},
\]

rather than the continuous range possible in classical fluids. Their stability, interactions, and collective dynamics reveal key properties of superfluidity, coherence, rotation, and quantum turbulence.

Examples include:

- **Superfluid helium:** Vortex lines in helium-4 and helium-3 carry quantized circulation and form lattices under rotation or tangled networks in quantum turbulence.
- **Nonlinear optics:** Phase singularities in optical fields act as vortex analogues; optical vortices carry quantized orbital angular momentum and can form in nonlinear optical media or photon-fluid systems.
- **Type-II superconductors:** Magnetic flux penetrates the material through Abrikosov vortices, each carrying a quantized flux \( \Phi_0=h/2e \). Their motion and pinning strongly influence electrical resistance and critical currents.
- **Ultracold atomic gases:** Bose–Einstein condensates and paired Fermi gases support quantized vortices, allowing direct imaging of vortex lattices and nonequilibrium vortex dynamics.

Thus, quantized vortices provide a unifying manifestation of phase coherence and topology across matter waves, electromagnetic fields, and superconducting condensates.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft an academic introduction to quantized vortices that includes the circulation formula \(\Gamma=\oint d\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf v(\mathbf r)\), discusses vortex lattices, pairs, and rings, and explains their observation in fermionic gases.
counterfactuals.output:
Quantized vortices are topological excitations that provide a direct manifestation of superfluid phase coherence. Writing the superfluid order parameter as \(\Psi(\mathbf r)=|\Psi(\mathbf r)|e^{i\phi(\mathbf r)}\), the velocity field is proportional to the phase gradient. The circulation around a closed contour is therefore

\[
\Gamma=\oint d\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf v(\mathbf r)=\kappa N,
\]

where \(N\in\mathbb Z\) is the phase-winding number and \(\kappa=h/M\) is the circulation quantum for condensed objects of mass \(M\). In a fermionic superfluid, where the order parameter describes pairs of atoms of mass \(m\), \(M=2m\) and hence \(\kappa=h/(2m)\). A vortex consists of a phase singularity surrounded by circulating flow, with the order-parameter amplitude suppressed in a core whose scale is set approximately by the coherence length.

Vortices occur in several characteristic configurations. Under sustained rotation, many vortices organize into an Abrikosov-like lattice, usually with triangular symmetry, whose areal density increases with angular velocity. Such lattices represent the superfluid analogue of rigid-body rotation when viewed on length scales large compared with the intervortex spacing. Vortices may also appear as vortex–antivortex pairs in effectively two-dimensional systems. Their creation, motion, and unbinding are central to nonequilibrium dynamics and to the Berezinskii–Kosterlitz–Thouless description of two-dimensional superfluidity. In three dimensions, vortex lines can close into vortex rings. These rings propagate through the fluid under their self-induced velocity and may be produced by stirring, phase imprinting, obstacle motion, or the decay of solitonic excitations.

The observation of quantized vortices in ultracold fermionic gases is particularly significant because it demonstrates macroscopic phase coherence associated with fermion pairing. Across the Bose–Einstein-condensate–BCS crossover, vortices can be nucleated by rotating an anisotropic trapping potential or by localized perturbations. Their cores are commonly detected as density-depleted regions after time-of-flight expansion, often with a rapid magnetic-field sweep that converts weakly bound Cooper pairs into tightly bound molecules and improves imaging contrast. Ordered arrays of such holes reveal vortex lattices, while appropriately resolved in situ or tomographic measurements can identify vortex pairs, bent vortex lines, and ring-like structures. Because density contrast can depend strongly on interaction strength, temperature, and imaging protocol, vortex identification is often supported by dynamical behavior, phase-sensitive measurements, or comparison with microscopic and hydrodynamic models. Collectively, these observations establish quantized circulation and provide a powerful probe of pairing, superfluid dynamics, dimensionality, and dissipation in strongly interacting fermionic matter.
